For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

A 1908 death falls after statewide registration began in 1906, so a state certificate should exist and typically names the father and the mother's maiden name. Read it first: it is the highest-yield direct parentage source already in hand.

The tree cites a 1860 U.S. Federal Census (S2) for Patrick but the project holds no assertions from it. United States, Census, 1860 is name-searchable. Find the Thomas Flynn household (born ca. 1818, Ireland) and Patrick (about 15), and record every member, which may name a mother and siblings and confirm Patrick is still in Thomas's home.

United States, Census, 1870 is name-searchable. By 1870 Patrick (about 25) may head or sit in his own household with a wife, so search for him under the birth range from every census age and also search the Thomas Flynn household if Thomas is still living. The 1870 schedule does not give relationships, so a household with a wife or with Thomas is a lead, not proof of parentage. Its wife's name and children's names feed the mother and sibling search.

Requested by the researcher: search the 1870 census on Ancestry for the same household searches as the FamilySearch 1870 item (Patrick under his birth range, and Thomas Flynn's household). Ancestry's transcription can differ from FamilySearch's index, so a household missed in one index may appear in the other. Treat any Ancestry hit as a derivative lead and verify it against the census image before relying on it.

United States, Census, 1880 is name-searchable and records each person's relationship to the head. If Thomas Flynn is living, his household should show Patrick as son; if it does, that directly places the child with the parent. Search the household of Thomas Flynn, and Patrick's own household, reading the relationship column.

A dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (born ca. 1818, Ireland) to Patrick's mother. Search Pennsylvania Church Marriages and Pennsylvania County Marriages, both name-searchable. The marriage supplies the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, which the project cannot yet tell. The window ends the year Patrick was born (ca. 1845). The marriage corroborates the couple as a unit but does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Note that the locality entry covers Pennsylvania only; if the marriage took place in Ireland, a locality survey is needed before searching there. Record the bondsmen and witnesses as FAN leads.

Patrick's baptism would name his father and mother. Search Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, name-searchable, for Patrick Flynn in the birth window, and for Thomas Flynn as father. The tree gives a birth in Ireland but the objective gives Pennsylvania, so search Schuylkill first and treat the Irish birth as unresolved. Catholic sacramental registers for Schuylkill are held by the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county, so a name-indexed hit may point to a parish register that needs to be requested. If the birth was in Ireland, this item cannot reach it; that needs a locality survey.

FAN item. Search baptisms and marriages of Thomas Flynn's other children, by Thomas Flynn as father, in Pennsylvania Births and Christenings and Pennsylvania Church Marriages. A sibling's record that names the same parents is direct parentage evidence for Patrick. The godparents and sponsors named in these records are the FAN associates to test.

A will or administration for Thomas Flynn, if he died in Schuylkill County, would name his children and so could name Patrick. The window is sized to Thomas's lifespan, not to the research window: born ca. 1818, he could die anywhere from the year Patrick was born to about 1905. Pennsylvania Probate Records is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Register of Wills dockets, not a name search. Schuylkill probate dates from 1811.

Patrick's own marriage record, if he married. The bride's and groom's parents are often named on the marriage register, and a marriage license may give the parents' names. Search Pennsylvania County Marriages and Pennsylvania Church Marriages for Patrick Flynn. Search every marriage found, because he may have married more than once.

Burial entries for Patrick (died 1908) and Thomas Flynn. A burial entry can state an age and a birthplace, and a family plot can list the parents or siblings. Pennsylvania Cemetery Records is name-searchable. Use the burial to check the age and birthplace the other records give, not as proof of parentage.

Fallback for the baptism item: if no baptism is found, a delayed birth record may give Patrick's birth date, place and parents' names. Pennsylvania Delayed Birth Records is name-searchable. Search the surname and the parents' names, not the birth year alone.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown: Patrick Flynn appears in the 1850 census in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. Co-enumeration is indirect evidence that supports but does not prove parentage. Post-1860 censuses, probate, and church records have not yet been searched.

planItems.rationale: Patrick Flynn's 1908 death in Schuylkill County is the one record of his life that usually names his father and mother. The tree's death fact (F2) already cites the Pennsylvania Death Certificates source (S3), but no assertion has been extracted from it yet, and the parentage link R1 also cites it. Read the attached certificate and extract the father's name, mother's name and informant. A state certificate exists because the 1906 statewide registration applied.

The 1850 census already places Patrick (age 5, born Ireland) in Thomas Flynn's household (dwelling 84). The 1860 United States Census (name-searchable) should show the same household with Patrick at about 15, testing whether Thomas and his wife stayed together and whether a mother is named. The 1860 schedule does not state relationships, so this item tests co-residence only. The birthplace conflict (tree and 1850 census say Ireland; the objective says Pennsylvania) is tested by the birthplace recorded here.

Dedicated parents' marriage search for Thomas Flynn (born about 1818, Ireland) and his wife. The Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 and Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 collections are both name-searchable. The marriage gives the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, so item 4 tests her other marriages. The couple's marriage shows they married before Patrick's birth but does not, alone, prove Patrick is their child. If the marriage took place in Ireland, this item finds nothing and the Irish origin search needs a locality survey.

Companion to item 3, testing whether the wife had an earlier or later marriage. No remarriage is suspected yet, but the surname she is recorded under is not yet tested against other marriages. Search Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 (name-searchable) for any marriage of a woman with her given name and Thomas Flynn's approximate household, and for her own birth or christening, which names her parents. Treat any surname found here as a prior or later name until a record confirms it.

Sibling and FAN search. Christenings in Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (name-searchable) for any child of Thomas Flynn and his wife, which would name both parents at once and so test the family unit. A sibling's entry supports parentage even when Patrick's own baptism is in Ireland. Look for a Flynn christening in the county with the same parents' names.

Fallback to item 5 if the civil-registry christening index yields nothing. Sacramental registers for Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875), not the county, so the Schuylkill County Church Records collection (name-searchable) may index only part of them. Search the parish registers at the parish or archdiocesan archive, where the original entries are held. The locality survey does not give a parish list, so identify the parishes from the 1850 census place before searching.

Census years after 1850 must be searched because the records disagree on Patrick's birthplace and the question depends on who lived with him. The 1870 United States Census (name-searchable) should show Patrick at about 25, tests whether Thomas is still living, and may show the wife's name or a stepmother if she remarried. Search Patrick and the household members, with birthplace variants.

The 1880 United States Census (name-searchable) is the first census that states each person's relationship to the head of household. If Thomas is alive in 1880 it can state that Patrick is his son, which is direct evidence for parentage. Search Patrick's household and any Flynn household with a Thomas at about age 62.

The 1900 United States Census (name-searchable) is the last census before Patrick's 1908 death. It asks for the number of children a mother has borne and their birthplaces, and it gives Patrick's birth month and year, which tests the 1845 estimate against the records. Search Patrick's own household, and any household of Thomas or the widow if Thomas is dead.

A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

facts.informant: Unknown household member reporting to census enumerator
facts.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. The household member who provided the name is unknown. Proximity is 'unknown' rather than 'household_member' because for names specifically, the enumerator may have read a sign, heard a neighbor, or made an assumption — the name fact doesn't necessarily require active reporting the way age/birthplace does.

facts.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn or wife)
facts.informant_bias_notes: Age and birthplace require active reporting by a household member — someone had to tell the enumerator these facts. Proximity is 'household_member' rather than 'unknown' because these facts could only come from someone in the household.

facts.informant: Census enumerator (witness to residence by visiting the dwelling)
facts.informant_bias_notes: For residence facts specifically, the enumerator is a direct witness — they physically visited the dwelling and recorded who lived there. This distinguishes residence from other census facts where the household member is the true informant.

facts.value: Listed in household of Thomas Flynn (head), position consistent with child
facts.informant: Inferred from household structure — no explicit informant for relationships in 1850 census
facts.informant_bias_notes: 1850 census does not state relationships; this assertion is inferred from household position and shared surname, not directly reported by any informant. The relationship is indirect evidence constructed by the researcher, not information provided by a census informant.

facts.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn himself) reporting to census enumerator
facts.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. As head of household, Thomas likely provided his own name, but the 1850 census does not identify the informant.

facts.informant: Ancestry transcriber (derivative of census enumerator)

items.notes: Found Patrick Flynn age 5 in household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, Schuylkill Co. Three other Flynn results examined — ages and locations don't match.
Ancestry index confirms same household. Transcription matches FamilySearch except Ancestry reads dwelling as 84, FamilySearch as 84 — consistent.
MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.

planItems.rationale: The 1850 household of Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84, already located by the 1850 name search in log_001) is recorded in the tree only through Patrick and Thomas. The log did not extract the other members, so the mother's given name is not in hand. Re-read the full household image for the wife and any other children. This identifies the mother, the first identifier the parentage search needs. The census is name-searchable, but the image is needed to read every member. 1850 names only the head as a relationship-free tally, so the wife's name is read as a household member, not as a stated relationship.

The tree cites the 1860 U.S. census (S2) as a source for the Flynn parent-child relationship (R1), but no log entry shows it was searched or extracted. Find Thomas Flynn's 1860 household: it is the first census that gives relationship to head, so it tests whether Patrick (about 15) is the son of Thomas and names the wife. The 1860 census is name-searchable.

FAN item. Patrick's household is the only evidence that places him with Thomas, so the neighbours on the same 1850 enumeration (the dwellings before and after dwelling 84) may be relatives: a brother, uncle or cousin of Thomas, or an Irish household from the same origin parish. Read the Flynn and Irish-born households next to dwelling 84 for a second Flynn household that could be a sibling or uncle of Thomas.

Dedicated parents' marriage item. Thomas Flynn (born about 1818 in Ireland) should have married the mother before Patrick's birth about 1845. The Schuylkill county marriage register is name-searchable. Search Thomas Flynn as groom with the bride unknown, because her name is not yet in hand. The marriage gives the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage. It corroborates Thomas as father by date, but does not by itself show Patrick is their child (that needs a record placing Patrick with them, from items 1, 2, 9 or 10). If the marriage was in Ireland, this item finds nothing and the Irish record item noted below takes over.

Companion to item 4 (pli_007). Thomas Flynn's later marriages are searched so that a remarriage does not get mistaken for the mother's marriage. A later marriage, or a bride whose surname differs between records, means the bride in item 4 may not be the mother's first husband's family. Check each marriage found for a bride's earlier name. The register is name-searchable.

Fallback for item 4 (pli_007). Schuylkill's Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia, so the sacramental marriage register is held at the parish or archdiocese, not the county. The church marriage collection is name-searchable, but it is an index and may be partial. Use it when no civil or county marriage is found for Thomas as groom.

Sibling baptisms. A baptism of a later child of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill names both parents directly, so it gives the mother's name without depending on her marriage. Search baptisms with Thomas Flynn as father. Pre-1846 baptisms in Pennsylvania are weaker because the parish register starts are uneven, so this item covers the years after Patrick's birth. The births and christenings collection is name-searchable.

Follows the family after 1860 to test whether Thomas and his wife are still together and whether Patrick, about 25, is listed with them. It also names any children not seen in 1850 or 1860. The 1870 census is name-searchable.

planItems.repository: Pennsylvania Department of Health (state death certificate)
planItems.rationale: Patrick's own death record. He died 12 March 1908, after the 1906 start of statewide certificates, so a state death certificate exists. It usually names the decedent's father and mother, which can give the mother's name and confirm Thomas as father. The tree cites the Pennsylvania death certificate source (S3), but no assertion was extracted from it, so read and extract it. The state death index is name-searchable; the certificate image is the record.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration. A will may name a wife and children, and so confirm Patrick as a son. The date window is set by Thomas's own lifespan (born about 1818, so he could have died any time from the 1845 birth of Patrick to about 1905), not by the research window. The statewide probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Register of Wills books, not a name search.

Fallback for item 10 (pli_013). The orphans' court kept estate dockets and distributions, which name heirs when a will was not found or when the estate was administered by the court. The date window follows Thomas's lifespan, as in item 10.

Deeds. A deed of sale by Thomas Flynn may carry a wife's dower release, which names her, and a deed after his death may name his heirs. The statewide wills and deeds collection is name-searchable. Search Thomas Flynn as grantor and grantee in Schuylkill County.

Thomas Flynn, born about 1818 in Ireland, may have filed naturalization papers. Declarations and petitions of this period often name a wife and minor children, which gives the mother's name and a dated list of children. Pennsylvania naturalization collections are name-searchable, but Schuylkill's court district must be confirmed before choosing the collection; this item searches Thomas Flynn under the Eastern and Middle District collections.

- Thomas Flynn (I2): birth about 1818 in Ireland (F3, starting tree). Parent-child relationship R1 to Patrick cites the 1850 census (S1), the 1860 census (S2) and the death certificate (S3).
- The log shows the 1850 census was located (log_001) and Ancestry confirmed the same household (log_002). MyHeritage gave no match (log_003). Those assertions place Patrick, age 5, in Thomas's household in Schuylkill County, but they do not name the mother. No assertion from the death certificate has been extracted yet.

Items, in order:
1. pli_004: 1850 household image (FamilySearch images), to read the wife and other members.
2. pli_005: 1860 census for Thomas's household, which the tree cites but nothing has searched.
3. pli_006: FAN item on the households next to dwelling 84 in 1850.
4. pli_007: Thomas Flynn's marriage, 1835–1846, to find the mother.

6. pli_009: church marriage fallback for pli_007.
7. pli_010: baptisms of later children, 1846–1865, which name both parents.
8. pli_011: 1870 census for Thomas's household.
9. pli_012: Patrick's 1908 state death certificate, which usually names parents.

11. pli_014: orphans' court estate records, fallback for pli_013.
12. pli_015: wills and deeds, for dower releases and heirs.
13. pli_016: naturalization of Thomas, under the Eastern and Middle District collections.

I set up a new research plan for the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were. It starts with the 1850 census household that already places him with Thomas Flynn, to find the mother's name, then looks at Thomas's 1860 and 1870 households, the marriage records, the baptisms of his other children, Patrick's 1908 death certificate, and Thomas's will, deeds and naturalization papers. The Irish birth and baptism records are not yet in the plan, because no survey covers Ireland yet. Searching begins with the FamilySearch items in that order.

items.rationale: The 1850 household of Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84, already located by the 1850 name search in log_001) is recorded in the tree only through Patrick and Thomas. The log did not extract the other members, so the mother's given name is not in hand. Re-read the full household image for the wife and any other children. This identifies the mother, the first identifier the parentage search needs. The census is name-searchable, but the image is needed to read every member. 1850 names only the head as a relationship-free tally, so the wife's name is read as a household member, not as a stated relationship.

The tree cites the 1860 U.S. census (S2) as a source for the Flynn parent-child relationship (R1), but no log entry shows it was searched or extracted. Find Thomas Flynn's 1860 household: it is the first census that gives relationship to head, so it tests whether Patrick (about 15) is the son of Thomas and names the wife. The 1860 census is name-searchable.

FAN item. Patrick's household is the only evidence that places him with Thomas, so the neighbours on the same 1850 enumeration (the dwellings before and after dwelling 84) may be relatives: a brother, uncle or cousin of Thomas, or an Irish household from the same origin parish. Read the Flynn and Irish-born households next to dwelling 84 for a second Flynn household that could be a sibling or uncle of Thomas.

Dedicated parents' marriage item. Thomas Flynn (born about 1818 in Ireland) should have married the mother before Patrick's birth about 1845. The Schuylkill county marriage register is name-searchable. Search Thomas Flynn as groom with the bride unknown, because her name is not yet in hand. The marriage gives the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage. It corroborates Thomas as father by date, but does not by itself show Patrick is their child (that needs a record placing Patrick with them, from items 1, 2, 9 or 10). If the marriage was in Ireland, this item finds nothing and the Irish record item noted below takes over.

Companion to item 4 (pli_007). Thomas Flynn's later marriages are searched so that a remarriage does not get mistaken for the mother's marriage. A later marriage, or a bride whose surname differs between records, means the bride in item 4 may not be the mother's first husband's family. Check each marriage found for a bride's earlier name. The register is name-searchable.

Fallback for item 4 (pli_007). Schuylkill's Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia, so the sacramental marriage register is held at the parish or archdiocese, not the county. The church marriage collection is name-searchable, but it is an index and may be partial. Use it when no civil or county marriage is found for Thomas as groom.

Sibling baptisms. A baptism of a later child of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill names both parents directly, so it gives the mother's name without depending on her marriage. Search baptisms with Thomas Flynn as father. Pre-1846 baptisms in Pennsylvania are weaker because the parish register starts are uneven, so this item covers the years after Patrick's birth. The births and christenings collection is name-searchable.

Follows the family after 1860 to test whether Thomas and his wife are still together and whether Patrick, about 25, is listed with them. It also names any children not seen in 1850 or 1860. The 1870 census is name-searchable.

items.repository: Pennsylvania Department of Health (state death certificate)
items.rationale: Patrick's own death record. He died 12 March 1908, after the 1906 start of statewide certificates, so a state death certificate exists. It usually names the decedent's father and mother, which can give the mother's name and confirm Thomas as father. The tree cites the Pennsylvania death certificate source (S3), but no assertion was extracted from it, so read and extract it. The state death index is name-searchable; the certificate image is the record.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration. A will may name a wife and children, and so confirm Patrick as a son. The date window is set by Thomas's own lifespan (born about 1818, so he could have died any time from the 1845 birth of Patrick to about 1905), not by the research window. The statewide probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Register of Wills books, not a name search.

Fallback for item 10 (pli_013). The orphans' court kept estate dockets and distributions, which name heirs when a will was not found or when the estate was administered by the court. The date window follows Thomas's lifespan, as in item 10.

Deeds. A deed of sale by Thomas Flynn may carry a wife's dower release, which names her, and a deed after his death may name his heirs. The statewide wills and deeds collection is name-searchable. Search Thomas Flynn as grantor and grantee in Schuylkill County.

Thomas Flynn, born about 1818 in Ireland, may have filed naturalization papers. Declarations and petitions of this period often name a wife and minor children, which gives the mother's name and a dated list of children. Pennsylvania naturalization collections are name-searchable, but Schuylkill's court district must be confirmed before choosing the collection; this item searches Thomas Flynn under the Eastern and Middle District collections.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

This is the first research plan for the question of who else Thomas and Sarah Hale had as children. It starts with the 1850 census for Greene County, Ohio, which is the first census to list every person in a household, and then checks the 1860, 1870 and 1880 censuses for children who left, married or were born later. It also looks at Thomas and Sarah's marriage record, the birth and baptism records for their children, and the records of Thomas's death and estate in 1868, since death and probate records often name heirs. response.objective: Besides their children Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, did Thomas Hale and his wife Sarah of Greene County, Ohio, have any other children? Identify each additional child.
response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

planItems.rationale: First census that names every household member. Find the Thomas Hale household (Thomas born about 1810 in Pennsylvania) and list every child under the head, with ages and birthplaces (birthplace first recorded in 1850). Any child not among Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph is a candidate. Read the adjacent households in the same enumeration for FAN leads. United States Census, 1850 is name-searchable (national collection in loc_001).

Second household check after 1850. Children who married or left between 1850 and 1860 may be absent, and younger children born after 1850 must appear here. Compare the list with the 1850 household and record any child who appears in one census but not the other. United States, Census, 1860 is name-searchable.

Thomas died in 1868, so this census should show Sarah as head or in a child's household. Each child still living, and the Hale household under Sarah or a child, is a candidate. United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable.

The 1880 census records each person's relationship to the head, so it can show whether a child living with Sarah is a son or daughter, or a grandchild or other relative. Sarah's household is the target if she was still living. United States, Census, 1880 is name-searchable.

The 1840 census names only the head of household. Everyone else appears as a tally in an age bracket, so this item cannot name a child. It is used to test whether the household's size and the number of children under 10, 10 to 19 and so on match the five named children, or suggest more. The 1830 census works the same way. United States, Census, 1840 is name-searchable.

The Thomas and Sarah Hale marriage record, searched under Greene County. It gives the marriage date, which bounds the earliest birth of any child, and it supplies Sarah's maiden name only if this was her first marriage. Search also any other Hale marriage in Greene County where Sarah is the bride. Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016 is name-searchable. The couple may have married in Pennsylvania, where Thomas was born; that jurisdiction has no locality entry yet.

Birth and christening records of children to Thomas and Sarah Hale, searched on both parents' names as parents. Ohio, Births and Christenings, 1821-1962 and Ohio, County Births, 1841-2003 are name-searchable. Births before 1841 are not in the county births collection, so the church item below is its fallback for those years.

Church baptism records give a child's parents when the civil birth record is missing or predates 1841. Ohio, Church and Civil Births and Baptisms, 1765-1947 and Ohio, Church Records, 1762-2008 are name-searchable. Search on Thomas and Sarah as parents, not only on the surname Hale. This is the fallback for the birth item, covering years before civil registration.

Thomas died in Greene County in 1868. The death or burial entry may name the informant, a surviving child, or the place of the family. Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001 and Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 are name-searchable. Search with no surname filter where the index is weak, since a daughter may have married and changed her name.

Thomas's estate file in the Greene County Probate Court. Per the locality quirk, probate moved from the Court of Common Pleas to the Probate Court in 1852, so the 1868 file is in the Probate Court series. Administration papers, inventory and distribution account commonly name each heir. Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the 1868 estate file, not a name search.

Sarah's death or burial, if she died after Thomas, may name her children as survivors or informants. Search Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001 and Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 on her name in Greene County. Her death date is unknown, so the window runs until the 1880 census and beyond. Her death record also helps place her household in the 1870 and 1880 censuses.

Pennsylvania records for the years before the family moved are not yet covered and need to be added later.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The census informant was likely a household member with firsthand knowledge (primary or indeterminate), while the death certificate informant (son-in-law) is clearly secondary for birth facts. Two contemporary sources outweigh one later recollection by a secondary informant.

planItems.rationale: Probate of Thomas Flynn (tree: birth ~1818, Ireland), the father named by the 1908 death certificate (a_013, secondary informant). A will or administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence and is the route ps_001 names for advancing to Proved. loc_001 lists Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 as browse-only, and the Register of Wills holds Schuylkill files from 1811, so this is an image browse of the county dockets. Date window runs from Patrick's birth year (1845) to about 60 years later, because Thomas could have died at any point in that span; the window is sized to his lifespan, not the subject's.

Name-searchable fallback for item 1: Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds (ca. 1700s-2017) is name-searchable, so a search on Thomas Flynn may surface a will or estate paper that the browse of Register of Wills dockets would take many hours to reach. Search Thomas Flynn with Schuylkill as the place, then Flynn with a wildcard for the given name if the first search fails. Pre-1811 files sit in Berks or Northampton and are out of this window.

Thomas Flynn's marriage record, which can give the mother's maiden name, and which is the only route to her name the project does not already hold. The mother's identity is unknown, so search every Thomas Flynn marriage in the county, not just the first. Pennsylvania Church Marriages and Pennsylvania County Marriages are both name-searchable. The marriage may have taken place in Ireland before emigration, in which case no Pennsylvania record exists; the date window covers a PA marriage after arrival and a remarriage. Corroborates the father only by its date relative to Patrick's birth (about 1845); it does not by itself link Patrick to Thomas. Any remarriage shows the surname may differ across records, so treat each marriage as a separate candidate for the mother.

Pennsylvania Births and Christenings is name-searchable. A baptism of a Flynn child to Thomas and his wife in Schuylkill places Patrick's siblings in the family, and a child baptised with Thomas as father and an Irish-born mother fixes the household as a unit. This also serves as the FAN item for parentage: godparents and sponsors named on these baptisms are the family's associates, and a sponsor who shares the Flynn surname may be a brother of Thomas. Search Flynn with father Thomas. Schuylkill's Catholic registers are held at the parish or the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county, so if the index lacks an entry, the parish register is the original to check.

Thomas Flynn's death or burial entry, which gives the year his probate could have opened and can state an age and birthplace to test the Ireland origin. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials (1720-1999) and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records (ca. 1700-ca. 1950) are both name-searchable. Pre-1906 deaths have no state certificate (loc_001), so these church and cemetery entries are the main routes to his death date.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record, dated to the years he was an adult in the county. Marriage records often name the groom's parents, and this would be an independent statement of his father's name, not a copy of the 1908 death certificate. Pennsylvania County Marriages and Pennsylvania Civil Marriages are name-searchable; the statewide civil register begins in 1893, so pre-1893 entries come from county and church sources.

Patrick Flynn's own burial entry, which the subject's died status calls for (Step 3). Pennsylvania Cemetery Records and Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials are name-searchable. The entry is placed in the county where he died in March 1908 and gives the burial parish, which points to the Catholic register that may hold a funeral entry naming the parents.

FAN item for parentage: marriages of other Flynn men and women in the county who may be Thomas's siblings or in-laws. The bondsmen, sureties and witnesses on those marriages (often the bride's father or brother) can name the same parents. Pennsylvania County Marriages is name-searchable; search Flynn as the surname with the place as Schuylkill and read each marriage's witnesses, not only the couple. A match between a witness and the probate or baptism names would be a lead to the family, not a conclusion about parentage.

Mode: add-new. The previous plan (pl_002) was already completed, and question q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?", is still only probable (ps_001), so I created a new active plan, pl_003. Nothing was superseded.

Survey facts the plan relies on:
- Tree: Thomas Flynn (I2) is recorded as Patrick's father (I1), born about 1818 in Ireland. The only source for that link is the 1908 death certificate, which names him through a son-in-law informant (a_013).
- The 1850 and 1860 censuses place Patrick in Thomas's household but do not state the relationship (a_004, a_010).
- Birthplace conflict c_001 is resolved in favor of Ireland.
- ps_001 names the open gaps: Thomas's probate, and the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses.

Plan pl_003, in execution order:
1. pli_006, probate, Schuylkill County, 1845-1905, FamilySearch (images). Browse of the Register of Wills dockets, the route to a will naming Patrick as a son.
2. pli_007, probate, Schuylkill County, 1845-1905, FamilySearch. Name-searchable fallback for item 1 through Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds.
3. pli_008, vital record, Schuylkill County, 1835-1880, FamilySearch. Every marriage of Thomas Flynn, to find the mother's maiden name and any remarriage.
4. pli_009, church, Schuylkill County, 1846-1865, FamilySearch. Baptisms of Flynn children to Thomas, which place Patrick's siblings and identify sponsors (FAN).
5. pli_010, cemetery, Schuylkill County, 1845-1905, FamilySearch. Thomas's death or burial entry, which also bounds the probate search.
6. pli_011, vital record, Schuylkill County, 1865-1908, FamilySearch. Patrick's own marriage, which may name his father independently of the death certificate.
7. pli_012, cemetery, Schuylkill County, 1908-1909, FamilySearch. Patrick's burial entry, the subject's own burial item.
8. pli_013, vital record, Schuylkill County, 1840-1875, FamilySearch. FAN item: witnesses and bondsmen on other Flynn marriages in the county.

Points for you to decide:
- No Irish item is planned. Patrick's baptism and his parents' marriage most likely took place in Ireland, and the project has no locality entry for Ireland. That needs a locality survey before those items can be written.
- I did not plan the 1870, 1880 or 1900 censuses, since you said censuses are done. The 1880 census would be the first to state relationships, so it is the census most worth adding later.

---

It then checks the burial and marriage entries for Thomas and Patrick, and finally the marriages of other Flynns in the county, whose witnesses may belong to the same family.

Next, the probate and church searches will run in the order of the plan, starting with the probate records for Thomas Flynn.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland, per 1850 census and the death certificate naming him as father of Patrick, tree F3) would have married the candidate mother before Patrick's ~1845 birth. The County Marriages collection is name-searchable and the Church Marriages collection is name-searchable for Schuylkill's Catholic parishes, which are under the Diocese of Philadelphia (loc_001). FAN item on the son-in-law. James Brown, who reported Patrick's birth and father on the 1908 death certificate (tree F2, S3), is a direct witness to family knowledge. His marriage to a Flynn daughter, in the County Marriages collection (name-searchable), may name the bride's parents, which would confirm Thomas Flynn as a father of a daughter and test the death certificate's secondhand parentage. Search Brown with the bride's surname Flynn and with Thomas Flynn as a possible parent.

FAN item on the household's children. Baptisms of Flynn children in Schuylkill parishes (Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, name-searchable) name both parents. A sibling of Patrick, or a child living in the household in 1850 or 1860, whose christening names Thomas Flynn and the mother would give direct parentage for Patrick through the family group. Search Flynn with father Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County, and check christenings for Patrick himself if any are found in the register period.

Census after the 1860 record, for the same household. Both collections are name-searchable.

FAN item on the 1850 neighbors. The 1850 enumeration of dwelling 84 (log_001) and the dwellings adjacent to it may hold Flynn kin, lodgers or Irish neighbors who were the household's informants (the 1850 census does not name the informant). Search by surname Flynn across Schuylkill first (name-searchable). Then browse the image group for dwellings 83 to 86 with volume_search for the census page, since neighbor households are not name-searchable.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration (the Register of Wills, held from 1811 per loc_001) would name his children, possibly including Patrick, and his widow. The window is sized to Thomas's lifespan (born ~1818, so possibly alive into the 1890s), not to the subject's research window. Pennsylvania Probate Records is browse-only (no name search), so this item is an image browse of the Schuylkill dockets for the Flynn surname, and the cited image group may need the county index first.

Thomas Flynn's own death or burial entry (Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, name-searchable). Burial and death entries often state age, birthplace and the widow's name, which would link the household to the wife named in the parents' marriage. Pre-1906 death registration is not statewide (loc_001), so rely on the Deaths and Burials and cemetery collections, and look for any entry giving a wife and children.

Thomas Flynn's naturalization papers (Pennsylvania naturalization collections, name-searchable for some courts). Declarations and petitions state birthplace, arrival and residence, and may name a wife and children. This tests the household's Irish origin and gives a family name list independent of the census informant. Schuylkill is served by more than one court, so search the Pennsylvania courts for the county and period.

The plan starts with the 1880 census to find out whether he had already arrived before 1882 and who lived with him. response.objective: Determine why Michael Sheahan relocated to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882
response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

planItems.rationale: The 1880 federal census is name-searchable (nationalCollections, United States, Census, 1880). It falls between the 1870 farmer record (log_001, outside Schuylkill) and the 1882 'miner' directory entry (log_002, Schuylkill). If Michael is in Schuylkill as a miner in 1880, the move predates the 1882 family-tradition date; if not, the move is later. The census also gives birthplace and relationship to head, which show whether he is Irish-born and whether he lived with kin or as a boarder.

FAN item: once the 1880 Schuylkill household is found (item 1), read its neighbors and boarders on the same enumeration page. Irish-born miners living near or boarding with Michael would show chain migration or a shared employer, which bears on why he moved.

log_001 located Michael as a farmer in the 1870 census outside Schuylkill, but the household's county was not extracted (assertion_count 0). Read that household to name the origin county and any household members who were Irish-born, so the move can be framed as leaving farm work for mining.

A marriage record in Schuylkill before 1882 would show the move already made and would give his residence and occupation at marriage. Search Pennsylvania County Marriages and Church Marriages (both name-searchable) for Michael Sheahan in Schuylkill. A marriage is also a dedicated record for a bride's family if one is found.

Browse-only Church Records volume for Schuylkill (English and German, 1842-1895). Used when item 4 finds no marriage. Parish registers in the coal region are browse-only per the locality guide, so this is an image-by-image browse of Catholic entries for Sheahan. Parish registers are held at the diocese or parish, so the volume is the only route if the online indexes miss him.

Baptisms of children born to Michael after the move record the father's occupation and residence. Search Pennsylvania Births and Christenings (name-searchable) for Sheahan entries 1882-1900 in Schuylkill. Pre-1906 civil birth registration does not exist statewide, so church baptisms are the route.

Schuylkill naturalization volume is browse-only (0% record-searchable). If Michael was foreign-born, a declaration of intention can give his arrival date and the date he began residing in the county, which tests the 1882 date directly. Browse image by image; no name search is available.

The Schuylkill deed volume is 22% record-searchable. The locality guide notes that coal-region land was usually leased from mining companies rather than bought by laborers, so a deed is unlikely but would show whether Michael bought or leased land in the county around 1882 and whether a company was involved.

Cemetery and Deaths and Burials records (both name-searchable) for Michael after 1882. A burial entry may give his occupation and the parish, and it shows whether he stayed in the county. Search with the surname variants from the 1870 and 1880 records.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

planItems.rationale: Tree survey: Patrick Flynn (I1) has a birth of about 1845 in Ireland (F1) and a death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (F2, cited to the death certificate); Thomas Flynn (I2) has a birth of about 1818 in Ireland (F3). The 1850 and 1860 censuses (log_001, log_004) place Patrick aged 5 and 15 in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, Schuylkill County. The 1880 census is the first post-1860 count that names relationship to head, so it can test directly whether Patrick (about 35) is still Thomas's son in the same household. Search the United States, Census, 1880 collection (name-searchable) for Patrick Flynn with birth range about 1840-1850, using birthplace Ireland OR Pennsylvania because the tree and the earlier searches disagree on birthplace; do not key on birthplace alone. Then search each household member of the Schuylkill entry for Thomas Flynn (about 1818 birth, Ireland). Only a household where Patrick is listed as son of Thomas counts toward parentage.

The 1870 census (United States, Census, 1870, name-searchable) is the first post-1860 count and falls between the 1860 record (log_004) and the 1880 count. Patrick would be about 25 and Thomas about 52. The 1870 schedule does not give relationship to head, so a match rests on the household composition: Patrick Flynn with birth range about 1840-1850 in the same dwelling or the next household as Thomas Flynn (about 1818, Ireland), with a shared Flynn household group. Treat co-residence as supporting, not proof of parentage, and record the dwelling and family numbers for comparison with 1860 dwelling 84. Search by the birth range re-derived from the 1850, 1860 and 1880 ages, not a single reading.

Patrick would be about 55 and was living until 1908 (death certificate, S3). The 1900 census (United States, Census, 1900, name-searchable) gives month and year of immigration and the mother-and-father birthplaces are not given, but it does name relationship to head, so it can show whether Patrick is living in Thomas's household or in a household headed by a relative such as the son-in-law James Brown, who gave the 1908 death information (log_005). Search for Patrick Flynn born about 1840-1850 in Ireland or Pennsylvania, then search each household member for Thomas Flynn (about 1818 birth; if Thomas is still alive he would be about 82). A 1900 household headed by Patrick's own household is a lead to note, not a confirmation of his parentage. Do not treat an absence of Thomas in 1900 as evidence he died before 1900 until the Schuylkill index is searched without a surname filter.

FAN item required on a parentage question. The death certificate (log_005) names son-in-law James Brown as the informant, so the household of Brown and his wife (Patrick's daughter, if identified) in the 1880 and 1900 Schuylkill censuses may show Patrick or Thomas living with them, or name neighbors who were kin. Search the 1880 and 1900 United States, Census entries for James Brown in Schuylkill County and note every household member and adjoining dwelling. Each record is a lead to Patrick's household and to Thomas, not an identification by surname alone; the rationale for any link must name the record that places the person with Patrick.
