response.objective: Find all children of Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps, whether recorded in Family Tree or not.
response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

Childs's own marriage or birth record naming her parents — pli_005 (Mary's birth record) and pli_006 (Benjamin and Mary's marriage record) cover this; (3) census items (1850, 1870, 1880) and a death/burial item for Harriet — all present as pli_007, pli_008, pli_009, pli_010; (4) a sibling test via church/baptism records — pli_011. The only possible gap is no explicit item for Clarisa Davis's other marriages, but she died in 1830 making another marriage after that impossible, and before 1816 (Benjamin's birth) she was already married to Peyton, so this omission is reasonable. The subagent set the earlier plan pl_001 to completed and created pl_002 as the active plan for q_001. Its report follows.

This plan will look for Harriet Phillips in the 1850, 1860, 1870 and 1880 census records for Thompson, then in Connecticut marriage, baptism, death and probate records, to show whether she was the mother, sister, aunt or in-law of Benj Phillips and whether she is connected to the Phipps family at all. The searches will go to the FamilySearch census and vital records first.

Would you like me to run the first plan item, pli_007, the 1850 census search?

response.objective: Find all children of Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps, whether recorded in Family Tree or not.
response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.narrationGuidance: Plain language for someone who has never done genealogy. No identifiers, file names, tool names or field names. Never write GPS, proof, proved or exhaustive: say genealogy standards; call an answer a conclusion when it is well established and a finding otherwise; say what we searched and what we could not reach. Never sound surer than the evidence was rated: say the records show it for a well established fact or relationship, probably for a likely one and possibly for a tentative one, and never write that someone is the parent, spouse or child of another without one of these. Say match or search result, never hit; never write ARK: name the record or link to it. Do not describe your own instructions or checks. Do not narrate between actions; report once when the step is done: what was found, in one paragraph, and what happens next in one sentence.

items.question: Who were the children of Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps (b. 1816 Thompson, Connecticut)?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The household censuses name the children living at home.
The 1850 census names every member of the household, so it lists the children at home that year.
The 1860 household lists any children at home between the 1850 and 1870 enumerations.
The 1870 household lists the children still at home.
The 1880 census states each member's relationship to the head.
Birth, death and marriage entries that name Benjamin or Mary as a parent can show a child no census caught.
His death and burial entries fix the end of the window and may name survivors.

planItems.rationale: Harriet Phillips (b. about 1800, Connecticut) is indexed in the 1860 Thompson dwelling of Benj Phillips (b. about 1815), but no 1850 household for that Phillips pair has been searched. The 1850 census names every member with age and birthplace but gives no relationship to the head, so any tie of Harriet to Benj must be inferred from surname, age and order unless another record states it. Also read the 1850 Benjamin J Phipps Thompson household already matched to the subject (log_001, not yet read) for a Harriet in it. Name-searchable.

Fan item. Mary S Phillips (b. about 1828) may be Mary L. Childs, the tree's wife of Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps, but that fit is unconfirmed. If Harriet is a mother, sister or aunt on the Childs side, she would appear in a Childs household in 1850 as a woman born about 1800. Search Childs households in Thompson for a Connecticut-born woman of that age. This tests whether Harriet belongs to the Childs family rather than the Phillips one. Name-searchable.

Open the indexed 1860 dwelling of Benj Phillips and read every person in it, then the dwellings listed immediately before and after it on the same enumeration page (fan). The 1860 schedule has no relationship column, so household order, ages and birthplaces are the only evidence of who Harriet is. Neighbouring households may hold Harriet's own husband, children or siblings under a different spelling. The earlier 1860 Phipps search returned nothing (log_002, log_009), so this item reads the Phillips dwelling directly. Name-searchable.

Find Harriet, born about 1800 in Connecticut, in 1870 Thompson households under Phillips and Phipps spellings, and read the 1870 Benjamin Phipps household already matched to the subject (log_003, ark MN7R-N8P) for a Harriet in it. The 1870 schedule gives no relationship to the head, so a shared household is corroboration only. Name-searchable.

The 1880 schedule states each member's relationship to the head, so it is the strongest test of who Harriet is if she is alive in 1880. Read the 1880 Benjamin Phipps household already matched to the subject (log_004, ark MFZQ-VND) and the 1880 Benj Phillips household, if found, for a Harriet born about 1800 and her stated relationship. A relationship of mother, sister, aunt or mother-in-law would settle the tie for that census. Name-searchable.

Marriage of Benjamin Phillips to Mary S (b. about 1828). Marriage entries often name the parents of both spouses. A parent named as Harriet would show her relationship to Benj or to Mary. If Mary had an earlier marriage, add that entry too, since a surname given in one marriage may not be her birth name. Name-searchable.

Baptism or birth entries for Benjamin Phillips (b. about 1815) and Mary S (b. about 1828) in Thompson. A baptism that names the parents is direct evidence of the relationship, and an entry naming Harriet as mother or sister would settle it for that child. Register coverage for Thompson is in the locality entry; check it before concluding a missing entry means no child. Name-searchable.

Death or burial entry for Harriet Phillips in Windham County, born about 1800. Death entries usually give age, birthplace and sometimes parents or the household she died in, which could fix her relationship to Benj Phillips or to the Childs family. Name-searchable.

Probate of a Phillips man in Thompson, or of Harriet herself if she was a widow. An estate file names heirs and states relationships, so it can settle whether Harriet is a widow, a mother or a sister. Search the Phillips surname in Windham County wills and deeds for heirs named as Harriet. Name-searchable.

All items are planned on FamilySearch collections that are name-searchable.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly identified the add-new mode, set pl_001 to completed (all items were completed), and created pl_002 as the active plan. The factual claims about the 1860 household (Benj b.1815, Mary S b.1828, Harriet b.1800, Connecticut) match the log entries. However, the per-test context requires that the plan's first items reach the relatives' other marriages — specifically Peyton Randolph Phipps (I2, d.1843) and his possible other marriages after Clarisa (I6, d.1830), and Mary L. Childs's (I4) own marriage or birth record to identify her parents. The plan entirely omits these required first items. Instead it jumps straight to census searches. The rationale for pli_008 (Childs households in 1850 census) is a reasonable FAN item but does not substitute for a marriage/birth record for Mary L. Childs that would name her parents. The plan also does not address Peyton's possible other marriages (he survived Clarisa by 13 years and could have remarried, producing a half-sibling of Benjamin who might be Harriet). These are concrete omissions of required content, not stylistic gaps.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The per-test context explicitly requires that before any further census search, the plan's first items reach relatives' other marriages: one marriage item for each parent of the head or spouse in the project tree covering that parent's other marriages (Peyton Randolph Phipps, I2, d.1843; Clarisa Davis, I6, d.1830 — so Peyton's other marriages after Clarisa's 1830 death), and a marriage or birth record for Mary L. Childs (I4) that names her parents. None of these items appear in pl_002. The plan goes directly to census searches (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) and then vital/probate records, but the required 'first items' targeting parental other-marriage records are entirely absent. This is a major omission of items the per-test context explicitly mandated.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All tool calls used live fixtures (matched.kind == 'live') with no fixture_not_found errors. The research_query calls correctly targeted section='questions', section='plans', and section='log' for q_001. The research_append calls correctly used op='update' to set pl_001 to completed and then appended the new plan with all nine items. No critical argument mismatches are visible. The expected_args fields are null (no fixture-declared expected args), so there is nothing to compare against for partial credit deductions.

dimensions.name: Record type selection
dimensions.rationale: The plan uses census records (pli_007–pli_011) to track Harriet across decades, vital records (pli_012–pli_014) for marriage, birth, and death entries, and probate (pli_015) for estate files naming heirs. Each record type is appropriate for the information need: census for household composition, vital records for parentage and relationship, probate for heir relationships. The rationales explain what each type provides. However, the plan is missing marriage records for Peyton Randolph Phipps's other marriages and a birth/marriage record for Mary L. Childs — record types that would have been vital records and are appropriate for the question. The absence of those items is a completeness gap rather than a wrong record type selection for what is present.

dimensions.name: Objective scope containment
dimensions.rationale: Every item in the plan is tied to identifying Harriet Phillips and her relationship to the 1860 household — which is the question's scope. The FAN item (pli_008, Childs households) explicitly states it tests whether Harriet belongs to the Childs family. The probate item (pli_015) targets Phillips estates to name heirs. No item pursues a relative's own facts for their own sake. The rationales consistently link each item back to what it would reveal about Harriet's identity and relationship to the subject's household.

dimensions.name: Sequencing logic
dimensions.rationale: The plan sequences census records chronologically (1850→1860→1870→1880) before vital and probate records, which is a reasonable order. Free/indexed FamilySearch sources are used throughout. However, the per-test context requires that marriage records for parents (Peyton's other marriages, Mary's parentage) come first — before further census searches — and those items are absent entirely. Within the items that exist, the 1860 census item (pli_009) correctly comes after the 1850 item, and the 1880 item (pli_011, which has relationship columns) is correctly noted as the strongest test. No fallback_for chains are used, which is a minor gap but not fatal given the items are largely independent searches. The date ranges cover the full window from 1850 to 1900.

dimensions.name: Jurisdiction accuracy
dimensions.rationale: All items correctly use Thompson, Windham, Connecticut as the jurisdiction for the 1850–1880 period. The probate item uses Windham, Connecticut (county level), which is correct for Connecticut probate records. Connecticut was a state throughout this period (1850–1900), so no pre-statehood issues arise. The jurisdictions match what existed in the target period.

The skill set pl_001's status to 'completed' (not 'superseded') before creating pl_002 as active. response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.objective: Find all children of Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps, whether recorded in Family Tree or not.
response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.rationale: The 1850 census names every member of the household, so it lists the children at home that year.
The 1860 household lists any children at home between the 1850 and 1870 enumerations.
The 1870 household lists the children still at home.
The 1880 census states each member's relationship to the head.
Birth, death and marriage entries that name Benjamin or Mary as a parent can show a child no census caught.
His death and burial entries fix the end of the window and may name survivors.

items.notes: Ad-hoc, user-requested child enumeration for Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps (I1). Top match Benjamin J Phipps, 1850 Thompson household (ark M68Y-B65), attached to subject, matchScore 0.74; read household next. Remaining hits are Phillips/Phelps surname-variant noise flagged needs-review.

Ad-hoc child enumeration. No Phipps Benjamin household in Thompson 1860 among the 50 ranked rows; top rows are Benj/Benjamin Phillips (surnameNotOnSubject, needs-review) and directory entries. Nil for Phipps under this query; Phillips rows not treated as the subject. Note the 1850 Benjamin entry is indexed as Phillips-variant in some rows, so a 1860 Phipps nil is a finding about this index, not proof of absence.
Ad-hoc child enumeration. Top match Benjamin Phipps, 1870 Thompson household (ark MN7R-N8P), attached to subject, matchScore 0.99, birth year 1816 matches. Read household next.

Ad-hoc child enumeration. Top match Benjamin Phipps, 1880 Thompson household (ark MFZQ-VND), attached to subject, matchScore 0.98, birth 1816, occupation Farmer, married. 1880 schedule states relationship to head. Read household next.

Ad-hoc. Spouse-anchored 1860 census search for a Phipps entry with Benjamin as spouse, no place filter as sent. 77,779 total pool; none of the 50 ranked rows is a Benjamin Phipps entry. Ranker: subjectResolvable false, no candidate above 0.01. Real nil for this query shape. The 1860 schedule has no relationship-to-head column; any family structure is inferred from surname, ages and order, not stated.

Ad-hoc child search anchored on father Benjamin Phipps, anyPlace Thompson, 1849-1878. Pool shows the 1850, 1870 and 1880 Benjamin Phipps Thompson entries and the indexed marriage of George Fairbanks Phipps (1902, Fitchburg MA; groom b.1867 Thompson; father Benjamin F. Phipps present). Other rows are Jason and Miranda Phipps entries or surname variants, flagged needs-review. Place-scoped; the recordCountry-anchored father search follows as a separate entry.

Ad-hoc child search anchored on mother Mary Childs, US-wide 1849-1878. Rows with mother Mary L. present include the George Fairbanks Phipps marriage 1902 (groom b.1867 Thompson, mother Mary L. Childs present) and Mary E. Phipps (b.1856, d. 9 Apr 1859 Thompson, mother Mary L. present, father Benjamin F. present). Other rows are unrelated Mary-named mothers.

Ad-hoc death search for the subject, 1893 Thompson. Confirms death 16 Aug 1893 in Thompson across the Connecticut Hale collection, Find a Grave and the Connecticut births index entry for Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps (b. 30 Jan 1816 Thompson, attached to subject). A Connecticut marriages entry (QPMQ-68VS) names a Benjamin F Phipps b.1817 d.16 Aug 1893 with parents Payton and Mary Phipps, not the subject's mother Clarisa; needs review, not adopted.

Ad-hoc 1860 census search for a Mary Phipps in Thompson. None of the 50 ranked rows is a Phipps entry with Benjamin or Mary; rows are Phillips and Phelps variants flagged needs-review. Ranker: subjectResolvable false, no candidate above 0.01. Real nil for this query; the 1860 Benjamin F. Phipps entry is not located under these names. The 1860 schedule has no relationship-to-head column; family structure would be inferred from surname, ages and order, not stated.

Ad-hoc childrenSearch follow-up, father Benjamin Phipps, US-wide 1849-1878, no place. Ranker: subjectResolvable false, no candidate above 0.01 against I1, so the pool does not resolve to the subject's family. Rows are Benjamin Phipps fathers in Massachusetts (Chelsea, Hopkinton), Virginia (Grayson), North Carolina, Indiana, Missouri and elsewhere, flagged as different Benjamins and not adopted. Needs review as a namesake pool.
Attempt blocked by the search service (User-Agent rejected by WAF); no results returned. Not a nil. Re-run under the variant searches below.

Spelling variant Pheaps, 1860 census scope Thompson CT. All 12 results are UK outgoing passenger lists, WWI draft, Iowa/Indiana records under unrelated names. No 1860 census entry for a Benjamin under this spelling. Ranker: no candidate scored above 0.01.

Spelling variant Phips with 1860 Thompson scope (place expanded to Thompson, Windham County and Nashaway). Ranked list is mostly vital and burial records for Benjamin F Phipps (b.1816, d.16 Aug 1893), not census. Surfaced one 1860 census entry, Benj Phillips (b.1815, Connecticut), Thompson, rank 8, attached to subject, surname not Phipps: needs-review. Read as one dwelling; family structure inferred from surname, ages and order, not stated. No 1860 Phipps census household found under this spelling.

Wife search, Mary Phipps in 1860 Thompson. Only page 1 read (20 of 21,729). Surfaced 1860 census entry Mary S Phillips, b.1828 Connecticut, in one dwelling with Benj Phillips (b.1815) and Harriet Phillips (b.1800); family structure inferred from surname, ages and order, not stated. Mary S b.1828 fits Mary L. Childs (tree birth 6 Jan 1828). Needs-review: surname Phillips, not Phipps; no children indexed in that dwelling. Other rows are Phelps and Phillips women, not this family.

Children test for Phillips in 1860 Thompson. Parent-name anchors do not appear on the 1860 census (no relationship column), so relative terms are unknown on these rows; family structure inferred from surname, ages and order, not stated. Results are other Phillips entries, including the Benj Phillips dwelling again (Harriet and Mary S). No child indexed there. Nil for children under this surname in this place.

Children enumeration, place-free, anchored on United States per childrenSearch guidance. Confirmed Mary E. Phipps, b.1856, d. 9 Apr 1859 Thompson CT (Connecticut Deaths and Burials, record F7V7-22Q), parents Benjamin F. and Mary L. Not in the tree. Also Charles Phipps b.1862, 1880 census Thompson household of Benjamin Phipps, mother Mary, already in tree. No other Phipps child of this couple found in the 1849-1866 window.

Children enumeration under Phillips surname, place-free, anchored on United States. No child linked to the Benjamin and Mary pair. Results are unrelated Phillips families in Massachusetts and elsewhere.

planItems.rationale: Identity of Harriet Phillips (b. about 1800, Connecticut) in the 1860 Thompson dwelling of Benj Phillips (b. 1815, Connecticut; record MHR9-JWT). The tree gives the subject's own 1849 marriage to Mary L Childs (b. 6 Jan 1828, Woodstock) in Webster, Massachusetts, but the 1860 dwelling indexes the household head and wife as Phillips. The marriage of Benj Phillips to his wife, in Connecticut Marriages, 1640-1939 (name-searchable), would name a bride and possibly a family tie for Harriet. Log_013 and log_014 treat the Phillips surname as unsettled, so this item tests whether that household is a Phillips family at all.

planItems.jurisdiction: Thompson and Windham, Windham County, Connecticut
planItems.rationale: Christenings of Harriet Phillips (about 1800) and of Benjamin Phillips (about 1815) in Connecticut Births and Christenings, 1649-1906 (name-searchable). dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly identifies the lifecycle state (pl_001 all completed, add-new mode), sets pl_001 to 'completed' (not 'superseded'), and creates pl_002 as active. The factual claims about the 1860 household (Benj b. 1815, Mary S b. 1828, Harriet b. 1800, Connecticut) match the scenario description. The claim that Harriet 'cannot be a child of the subject' is correct given her ~1800 birth vs. Benjamin's 1816 birth. However, the plan has a significant correctness gap: the per-test context requires that the first items reach the relatives' other marriages — specifically Peyton Randolph Phipps's other marriages (his wife Clarisa died 1830, so he could have remarried before his 1843 death), Clarisa Davis's other marriages, and Mary L. Childs's birth/marriage record naming her parents. The plan does include pli_009 for Peyton's earlier marriage (1795-1813), but misses: (1) Peyton's later marriage after Clarisa's 1830 death (which could produce a half-sibling Harriet born ~1800 is impossible from a post-1830 marriage, but a step-sibling scenario is missed), (2) Mary L. Childs's parents are not in the tree and the per-test context explicitly requires an item for her own marriage or birth record naming them — this is entirely absent from the plan. The plan also treats Harriet as potentially a half-sibling of the subject via Peyton's earlier marriage, but Harriet born ~1800 and Peyton born 1789 would make him ~11 at her birth — this is implausible but not flagged. More critically, the plan omits any item for Mary Childs's parentage, which the per-test context explicitly requires.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The per-test context explicitly requires: 'one marriage item for each parent of the head or spouse who is in the project tree, covering that parent's other marriages (Peyton Randolph Phipps, I2, died 1843, his wife Clarisa, I6, having died in 1830; Clarisa herself). Mary L. Childs's (I4) parents are not in the project tree, so an item for her own marriage or birth record that names them belongs among those first items.' The plan includes pli_009 for Peyton's earlier marriage (pre-1813) but misses: (1) Peyton's later marriage after Clarisa's 1830 death — Harriet born ~1800 couldn't be from this, but a step-sibling from a post-1830 remarriage is a candidate the plan should address; (2) Clarisa Davis's own other marriages or parentage; (3) most critically, Mary L. Childs's birth or marriage record to identify her parents, who are not in the tree. The per-test context explicitly names this as a required item. The plan has 8 items covering census, church, vital, and probate records but omits the Mary Childs parentage item that the instructions specifically call for.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

- The tree records Mary L Childs (born 6 Jan 1828, Woodstock, Connecticut) as married to Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps on 24 Mar 1849 in Webster, Massachusetts. Her parents are not in the tree.
- The tree places Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps in Thompson in 1850, 1860, 1870 and 1880, and Mary L Childs in Thompson in 1850 through 1880.
- The 1860 Benj Phillips dwelling (log_013, log_014) lists Harriet Phillips (born about 1800, Connecticut), Mary S Phillips (born about 1828, Connecticut) and Benj Phillips (born about 1815, Connecticut). Mary S's birth year fits Mary L Childs, but the surname differs, so this is unconfirmed.

Plan items (pl_002, in order):
1. pli_007: birth or baptism of Benj Phillips, about 1812-1818, Windham, Connecticut. Names his parents, which may show whether Harriet is his mother.
2. pli_008: birth or baptism of Mary Childs, 1826-1830, Woodstock, Connecticut. Names her parents, which may show whether Harriet is her mother.

Fallback relationships: none. All items are name-searchable collections except none are browse-only.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The plan correctly identifies the lifecycle state (pl_001 all items completed → set to completed, new active pl_002 created). The tool calls confirm pl_001 was updated to 'completed' and pl_002 was successfully written. The factual claims about the 1860 household (Harriet b. ~1800 CT, Mary S b. ~1828 CT, Benj b. ~1815 CT) match the log entries. However, the plan has a significant correctness defect per the per-test context: the first items should reach the relatives' other marriages — specifically Peyton Randolph Phipps (I2, d. 1843) and Clarisa Davis (I6, d. 1830) who are in the project tree as Benjamin's parents. Peyton died in 1843 and Clarisa in 1830, so Harriet (b. ~1800) could be a sibling of Benjamin's father or a relative from Peyton's side. The plan instead starts with Benjamin's own birth record (pli_007) and Mary Childs's birth record (pli_008), which are reasonable but miss the required first items: Peyton's other marriages and Clarisa's other marriages. The per-test context explicitly states 'the plan's first items reach the relatives' other marriages: one marriage item for each parent of the head or spouse who is in the project tree.' This is a concrete defect — the plan omits items for Peyton Randolph Phipps's other marriages and Clarisa Davis's other marriages, which are required by the per-test context. Additionally, pli_009 (marriage of Mary's parents) is conditioned on pli_008 finding the parents' names, which is a reasonable dependency, but the rationale for pli_003 correctly notes this dependency. The plan also does not address Peyton's siblings or Clarisa's family as candidates for Harriet, missing the in-law and step-relative candidates the per-test context requires.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The plan addresses several important avenues: birth records for the household head and Mary Childs, marriage records in CT and MA, census records across 1850-1880, Harriet's death record, and a FAN/neighbor search. However, per the per-test context, the plan must include items for the other marriages of Peyton Randolph Phipps (I2, in the tree, d. 1843) and Clarisa Davis (I6, in the tree, d. 1830) — these are the parents of the household head (Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps) who are in the project tree. Harriet born ~1800 in CT could be a sibling of Peyton or Clarisa, or a relative from their families. The per-test context explicitly requires 'one marriage item for each parent of the head or spouse who is in the project tree, covering that parent's other marriages.' Neither Peyton's other marriages nor Clarisa's other marriages appear as plan items. This is a concrete, named omission that the input state (the tree showing I2 and I6 as Benjamin's parents) made obvious. The plan also does not consider Harriet as a possible sibling of Peyton or Clarisa, or as a step-relative. These are significant gaps given the explicit per-test requirement.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All tool calls used live fixtures (matched.kind == 'live') with no fixture_not_found errors. The research_query calls for 'plans' and 'log' sections are appropriate. The tree_query for I4 and I1 with relevant fact types is well-targeted. The research_append calls correctly update pl_001 to 'completed' and create pl_002 with plan items. One call was rejected by the tool's own validation (jurisdiction naming two places), and Claude immediately corrected it by splitting into separate items — a clean single recovery. The final persisted state is valid per the tool's confirmation (ok: true, validation valid: true). No critical arg errors.

dimensions.name: Record type selection
dimensions.rationale: The plan uses vital records (birth, marriage, death) and census records throughout. Vital records are appropriate for identifying parents and establishing identity; census records are appropriate for tracking household membership across decades. The death record for Harriet (pli_016) is well-chosen as it would name her parents and husband. The FAN/neighbor census search (pli_017) is appropriate for an identity question. Each item's rationale explains what specific information the record type provides. However, the missing items for Peyton's and Clarisa's other marriages would also be vital records — their absence is a completeness issue, not a record type selection issue. The record types chosen for the items that are present are all appropriate.

dimensions.name: Objective scope containment
dimensions.rationale: Most items are well-scoped to identifying Harriet Phillips. The birth record for Benjamin (pli_007) is tied to identifying whether Harriet is his mother. The birth record for Mary Childs (pli_008) is tied to identifying whether Harriet is her mother. The marriage records (pli_009, pli_010, pli_011) are tied to understanding Mary's family connections. The census items (pli_012-pli_015) directly track Harriet across decades. The death record (pli_016) directly identifies Harriet. The FAN search (pli_017) is explicitly tied to finding Harriet's relationship. However, pli_009 (marriage of Mary's parents) and pli_010/pli_011 (Mary's marriages) are somewhat speculative — the rationale for pli_010 suggests Mary might have had a second husband named Phillips, which is a stretch given the evidence. The rationale for pli_009 depends on pli_008 finding parents' names first, which is noted. Overall, items are mostly tied to the question's subject (Harriet's identity), though some rationales leave the link slightly implicit.

dimensions.name: Sequencing logic
dimensions.rationale: The plan places vital records (birth/marriage) before census records, which is reasonable since they name parents directly. The 1880 census (pli_012, seq 6) is placed before 1870 (pli_013, seq 7), 1860 (pli_014, seq 8), and 1850 (pli_015, seq 9) — this is reverse chronological for the census items, which is defensible since 1880 has the relationship column and is most informative. However, the 1860 census re-read (pli_014, seq 8) is placed after the 1880 and 1870 censuses, even though the 1860 record is already known and would be the logical starting point for understanding Harriet's position. More significantly, pli_009 (marriage of Mary's parents) is correctly sequenced after pli_008 (Mary's birth record) since it depends on the parents' names. The date ranges cover the full window from 1812 to 1900. No fallback_for chains are used, which is a gap — the plan notes 'Fallback relationships: none' but some items (like the CT vs MA marriage searches) are natural fallbacks for each other. The sequencing is mostly reasonable but lacks explicit fallback chains.

A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

Mode: add-new. The earlier plan for q_001 (pl_002) had all its items completed and the question is not yet proved, so I wrote a new active plan, pl_003, and left pl_002 unchanged.

Question: q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

Facts already in the project that shape the plan:
- Patrick Flynn (I1): birth about 1845 in Ireland (F1). Death 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County (F2).
- Thomas Flynn (I2): birth about 1818 in Ireland (F3). Recorded as Patrick's father (R1).
- 1850 census (log_001): Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household. The relationship is inferred, not stated (a_004).
- 1860 census (log_004): Patrick, age 15, in Thomas Flynn's household. Again inferred (a_010).
- 1908 death certificate (log_005): names Thomas Flynn as father. The informant is son-in-law James Brown, a secondary informant (a_013).
- The birthplace conflict is open: the censuses say Ireland, the death certificate says Pennsylvania. The proof summary (ps_001) rates parentage Probable, not Proved, and lists the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and Thomas's probate as unsearched.

Plan items, in order:
1. pli_006: 1880 census, Schuylkill County (FamilySearch). The first census to state relationship to head.
2. pli_007: 1870 census, Schuylkill County (FamilySearch).
3. pli_008: 1900 census, Schuylkill County (FamilySearch).
4. pli_009: Mortality schedules 1850–1880, to learn whether and when Thomas died.
5. pli_010: Parents' marriage, Thomas Flynn and Patrick's mother, 1835–1846 (FamilySearch). This is the dedicated parents'-marriage item. The mother is not yet identified.
6. pli_011: Thomas Flynn's later marriages, 1846–1880 (FamilySearch). This tests whether the mother was his first wife.
7. pli_012: Patrick's burial entry, 1908 (FamilySearch). This is the subject's own burial record.
8. pli_013: Thomas Flynn's probate, 1850–1900 (county courthouse, browse-only). A will naming Patrick would be the strongest direct evidence.
9. pli_014: Flynn baptisms, 1840–1865 (FamilySearch). This is the FAN item for siblings, who would name the same parents.
10. pli_015: Marriage of James Brown to a Flynn bride, 1860–1908 (FamilySearch). This is the FAN item for the death-certificate informant.
11. pli_016: Irish baptism, 1840–1846, parish not yet identified (repository other). Only usable once a parish is named.

Not planned: a FamilySearch hints item, because Patrick has no ark in the tree. The military and naming-customs wiki pages do not apply, since Patrick was born in the British Isles and the surname is not compound.

Plan pl_003 for the parentage question is now active, with eleven items. The first step is the 1880 census for Schuylkill County, where Thomas Flynn's household should show whether Patrick is recorded as his son.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

planItems.rationale: Read the full household listing of the Kearney household in which the 1900 census image was already located (log_002). That image gives Bridget as mother of 9 children with 2 living, but names only Ellen Doyle so far. Read every member and their birth year and birthplace: children born before 1879 (the Kearney marriage, log_001) are the Doyle children sought; children born 1880 or later are Kearney children and must be separated out. Collection 1325221 (United States, Census, 1900) is name-searchable and is the source of the image.

Find the Martin Kearney and Bridget household (married 1879, log_001). The 1880 census gives each member's relationship to head, so Doyle children living with the couple should appear as stepchildren, which tests whether they are Bridget's by John Doyle. Collection 1417683 (United States, Census, 1880) is name-searchable. Also search for a Doyle household with Bridget or John in case the children stayed with the first husband.

Find the first marriage of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran, which bounds the birth window of their children (Ellen Doyle's own marriage record, log_003, already names them as parents). Bridget was born about 1838 in Ireland, so the marriage probably falls in the late 1850s or 1860s. Search County Marriages 1775-1991 (collection 1589502) and Church Marriages 1682-1976 (collection 2466360), both name-searchable, under Doyle with spouse Halloran. A marriage register entry may also give the parish, which points to the baptism register to search in item 6.

Find the John Doyle household with Bridget and their children, when the children were under about 15. Collection 1438024 (United States, Census, 1870) is name-searchable. Search Doyle with spouse Bridget and with Bridget Halloran as a possible transcription variant. Birthplace appears in this census, so Irish birthplaces help confirm the household.

Find the John Doyle household with Bridget and any earliest children, in the first years of the marriage. Collection 1473181 (United States, Census, 1860) is name-searchable. Search the name Doyle with the age range of Bridget (born about 1838) and check each household member's age against the children's birth years implied by the marriage date from item 3.

Find baptisms of children of John Doyle and Bridget (Halloran). The baptism entry names both parents and is the most direct evidence of each child. Search Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (collection 1681005), name-searchable, for the surname Doyle with mother Bridget and father John. The locality entry notes that Catholic sacramental registers are kept at the parish or diocese, not the county, and the indexed collection may not cover every parish, so item 7 and item 8 are the fallbacks.

Browse the image groups of Schuylkill-area Catholic parish baptism registers that the name index does not cover, for the Doyle entries. The locality entry says the anthracite coal region church films are browse-only and must be read image by image. Use volume_search to find the parish registers covering the Pottsville and Minersville area and the years from item 3. This is the fallback for item 6 and covers the Diocese of Philadelphia parishes, which kept Schuylkill.

Full-text co-occurrence search of parish register text for the surnames Doyle and Halloran appearing together, run across the corpus without a collection filter. Priests and clerks may have written the parents' names in forms the name index does not hold, so this catches a baptism that item 6 misses. This is the fallback for item 6 and is run through the full-text search skill.

If John Doyle died between 1850 and 1880, the Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules (collection 3512181, name-searchable) name the decedent and the month of death in the household. This narrows the year of John's death, which bounds the births of children after it and the probate item below. Search Doyle in Schuylkill.

Find burials of Doyle children who died young. Of the 9 children Bridget bore, only 2 were living in 1900 (log_002), so most died in childhood, and their burial entries may name the mother. Search Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 (collection 3535178) and Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 (collection 3743478), both name-searchable, for Doyle in Schuylkill County.

John Doyle's estate file and any guardianship of minor children, held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills (available from 1811, per the locality entry). The file names heirs and sometimes the minor children. The date range runs to 1900, covering John's probable death in the decades after the marriage, and it follows his lifespan rather than the subject's. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill dockets.

If John Doyle was an immigrant from Ireland, his naturalization papers (declaration or petition, which list a wife and minor children) can name the children. The federal court covering Schuylkill County for that date must be confirmed. Search Pennsylvania, Eastern District Court, Naturalization Records, 1795-1952 (collection 1937344) and Pennsylvania, Middle District Court, Naturalization Records, 1901-1992 (collection 5000058), both name-searchable, for John Doyle.

The later marriages of Doyle children name their mother (Bridget Halloran or Bridget Doyle) and sometimes the father, which can confirm a child not otherwise found. Search Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 (collection 1921317) and Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (collection 2466357), both name-searchable, under Doyle with mother Bridget, and check the listed parents against the couple.

Bridget's own death record and obituary (after 1900) can name surviving children and her parents, which tests the 1900 count of 2 living. Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (collection 2255317) and Schuylkill Haven, Funeral Home Obituary Cards, 1914-2007 (collection 3021637) are name-searchable. The date range runs past the locality entry's 1900 end because Bridget was alive then.

FAN item. Ellen Doyle's own death record or obituary may name her full siblings, which tests whether the other children share both parents. Her marriage record (log_003) names John Doyle and Bridget Halloran as her parents. Search Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (collection 2255317) and Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 (collection 3535178), both name-searchable, for Ellen Doyle, with the death window beginning at her marriage date.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

planItems.rationale: The tree holds only Mary Dawson's birth as 'about 1772, Lincolnshire, England' (fact F1) with no parents, no source and no baptism. A christening names the father and often the mother, so it is the first record to search for her parentage. loc_001 lists 'England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975' (collection 1473014) as name-searchable; its quirk is that it is a partial Legacy index, so a nil result is not proof that no christening exists. The date window allows for an age uncertainty around 1772.

planItems.jurisdiction: Lincolnshire, England (parish of the christening, once found; otherwise every parish of the county in turn)
planItems.repository: other: Lincolnshire parish register (image browse at the county archive or on FamilySearch, to be located in the catalog)
planItems.rationale: Fallback for item 1. Because loc_001's collection is a partial index, a missing christening there must be checked against the parish register image itself before it is treated as absent. No plan-level volume search returned a Lincolnshire image group for this period, so the register must be found by parish through the catalog; the locality guide's register start dates are not in the entry and should be read before concluding the baptism is out of reach.

Mary's own marriage, a generic search on her name, is planned because a baptism may not exist if the register start date falls inside her birth window, and marriage entries sometimes give the bride's father's name and her parish of residence. This is a lead to her parents, not proof of them. Search name-searchable collection 1473014 for Mary Dawson; the date window is her likely marrying age.

Parents' marriage, to be keyed once a candidate father is named by item 1, 2 or 3. It supplies the mother's maiden name only if that marriage was her first, so every marriage found for her must be checked. It corroborates a father named only indirectly, but it does not by itself prove that Mary is their child; a record placing her with the parents is still needed. Dependency: this item waits on the candidate's name, so it is sequenced after the christening and her own marriage.

FAN item. Baptisms and marriages of the Dawson family in the same parish, and of any sibling of Mary, name the same parents and the godparents, who are associates. Required on a parentage question. Searches the surname Dawson within the parish, and any sibling's christening that names the same father or mother, could show Mary's parents even if her own christening is missing.

planItems.jurisdiction: Lincolnshire, England (diocese and court that held the candidate father's will)
planItems.repository: other: Lincolnshire probate records (images, to be located in the locality guide's record_types)
planItems.rationale: A will or administration naming Mary as a daughter would be direct parentage evidence. The window is sized to the father's lifespan, not the subject's: a father of a child born about 1772 could die anywhere from then to about 1835. Probate is usually browse-only, so this is an image search of the Lincolnshire probate series by surname, not a name index search.

planItems.rationale: The subject's own baptism (tree fact F1: birth 1792, Württemberg, Germany, no source attached) is the first record that can name her parents. Search the name-searchable collection 'Germany, Births and Baptisms, 1558-1898' (loc_001) for Anna Margaretha Bauer, with the second given name Margaretha alone as well, per the locality quirk on German double given names. Her baptism entry is the most likely place the father and mother are named together. The register start of 1558 is well before the birth, so the baptism should exist; the record is not yet confirmed to hold the parish.

Fallback for item 1. If the name index does not return the subject's baptism, browse the image register of the parish or Protestant/Catholic church for the birth year directly, since the indexed collection may omit the entry. The volume search for Germany returned no image groups in this session, so the parish and register must be identified from the FamilySearch Catalog before browsing.

A dedicated search for the parents' marriage, which supplies the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage and corroborates a father named only indirectly. It proves the couple married but does not by itself show that the subject is their child. Search 'Germany Marriages, 1558-1929' (loc_001) on the surnames of the candidate parents once item 1 names them. Until then, search the surname Bauer as the bride's or groom's surname within the date range. Because the mother's earlier marriages are not excluded, item 6 covers them.

FAN item: baptisms of the subject's siblings, and of the godparents and witnesses named in the subject's own baptism. A sibling's baptism naming the same parents tests parentage independently of item 1. Godparents named in item 1 are also relatives or associates whose records may name the family. Search the same 'Germany, Births and Baptisms, 1558-1898' collection once item 1 gives a parent's name, and on the surname Bauer for the candidate family.

A father's probate or estate inventory, which may name the subject as a child. Test whether the mother named in item 3 had an earlier marriage. A surname that differs between the subject's records would show a remarriage. response.objective: Find the birth or baptism record of Hoval Hansen, also known as Haaval Hansen or Håval Ziener, born approximately 1780 in Kongsberg, Norway, and died in Trysil, Norway 18 August 1860.
response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

For the 1860 burial, the primary browse volume is 008679203_003 (Trysil church records 1814–1877, 325 images) — must be browsed image by image.

The Trysilboka farm book (Lillevold et al., FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l, multiple volumes) provides farm-level genealogical data for Trysil with personal name indexes in vols 1–3, 7–8 — check for Ziener/Hansen households.

Norwegian conscription/levy rolls (lægdsruller) began 1789 — a male born ~1780 would be enrolled under his father's name from approximately age 9, providing direct parentage evidence; access via Riksarkivet and Digitalarkivet.

Probate volumes at FS Catalog cover Sør-Østerdal only to 1853; for an 1860 estate use the Norway Probate Index Cards (FS col 1661306) to locate the reference, then retrieve the actual volume from Riksarkivet or Digitalarkivet.
Trysil Frimenighet (dissenter congregation) kept separate registers 1858–1920 at Digitalarkivet — check if subject had dissenter affiliation.
All Kongsberg church record volumes at FamilySearch are browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable); browse image by image for pre-1800 baptisms.

The national indexed extract (Norway Baptisms, col 1467014) has 28,370 Kongsberg records searchable but coverage of the 1780s period may be incomplete; a nil result is a reason to browse, not a conclusion.

Prime FamilySearch volume for a ~1780 baptism is 008680156_003 (church records 1769–1782, 382 images, browse-only); the same register is available at Digitalarkivet under Kongsberg/Kongsberg Parish Church Records 1696–1969.

Kongsberg was an industrial mining town dominated by the Kongsberg Sølvverk (royal silver mine, founded 1624); many residents were miners, and Low German occupational terms pervaded local naming — the alias 'Ziener' may derive from mining terminology.

Lægdsruller (military levy rolls) for this jurisdiction began 1789; a male born ~1780 would be enrolled ~1789–1796 directly under his father's name — direct parentage evidence alongside the baptism register.
Before 1760, Kongsberg was within Akershus amt; records from 1624–1759 are filed under Kongsberg, Akershus, Norway — relevant if the birth search must be widened beyond a strict ~1780 window.
Probate jurisdiction was the Kongsberg Byfogderi (Skifterett Kongsberg by); skifteprotokoller 1739–1851 are browse-only at FamilySearch Catalog (no. 437559) and at Digitalarkivet.

items.question: Where and when was Hoval Hansen (also known as Haaval Hansen and Håval Ziener, died 18 August 1860 in Trysil, Hedmark, Norway) baptized, and who were his parents?
items.rationale: This question directly restates the research objective. A baptism is a single event whose register entry typically yields date, place, and parents' names together. The specific death date and place (18 Aug 1860, Trysil) is the firmest anchor: Norwegian burial registers of this era routinely record age and birthplace (fødested), providing the bridge back to the Kongsberg parish baptism registers. For a birth circa 1780, civil registration postdates the event by ~34 years; the Lutheran ministerialbok (parish registers) for Kongsberg prestegjeld are the primary record class and are substantially digitized on Digitalarkivet.

planItems.rationale: Primary route to the baptism. The tree (I1, Living Hansen) holds no birth or baptism fact, no parents and no sources, so nothing here is yet established. Norway Baptisms, 1634-1927 (collection 1467014) is name-searchable and covers Kongsberg per loc_002. Search the given name as Hoval, Haaval and Håval, and the alias Ziener, with a birth window around 1780. loc_002 notes that coverage of the 1780s may be incomplete, so a nil result leads to item 2 and is not a conclusion. Parents' names are read from the entry if it gives them.

Fallback for item 1. The Kongsberg church volume 008680156_003 (1769-1782) is browse-only per loc_002, with 0% name indexing, so browse it image by image for the baptism entry. Digitalarkivet holds the same register under Kongsberg Parish Church Records 1696-1969. Also check Elverum prestegjeld for an earlier birth, since loc_001 says records before the 1780 Trysil split are filed there.

The subject's own burial entry for 18 August 1860. The Norway Burials, 1666-1927 collection (1468081) is name-searchable per loc_001. Burial registers of this era usually state age and birthplace (fødested), which can give the Kongsberg origin the baptism search needs. This item is required because the subject died and a birth register search alone may not succeed. Search the variant names above and Ziener.

Fallback for item 3. The primary Trysil church volume 008679203_003 (1814-1877, 325 images) is browse-only per loc_001 and must be browsed image by image for August 1860 burials. Use it if the indexed burial search returns nothing.

Estate reference for the subject's death in 1860. response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org)
The typical Spanish name has four parts: two given names, the father's surname and the mother's surname. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Naming_Customs)

It corroborates the father only if the child is placed with the parents elsewhere; the marriage alone does not prove the subject is their child. If she did, the marriage record in pli_003 may give a later surname and not her birth name, so this item searches her other marriages under her surname from her own civil marriage entries. This tests whether the surname given in pli_003 is her first. Search across the mother's surname variants, because the first surname is the only one usually indexed.

Norwegian name spellings were set by the recorder and vary between records (the wiki's example: the given name Sivert written as Syver, Sjur, Siver, Sifuer or Siffuer) — search given-name spelling variants, not just the tree's spelling, before concluding a nil.
