planItems.jurisdiction: Meland sokn, Hamre prestegjeld, Hordaland, Norway
planItems.rationale: Confirms the tree's only fact about the subject: the Birth fact (May 1745, Hestdal, Meland) in the project tree has no source attached. The Hamre baptism register (Norway Baptisms, 1634-1927, name-searchable per the Norway locality entry) gives her father's given name (Halstein, per the patronymic Halsteinsdatter), her mother, and her sibling names. Those names are the identifiers the marriage search needs and the FAN names for item 4. Norwegian patronymic customs (Norway_Naming_Customs): the surname is derived from the father's given name, and Hestdal is a farm name, which is residence and goes in the locality, not the surname. Search given-name variants (Unna, Una, Unne) and the abbreviated surname form (Halsteinsd., Halstensd.).

planItems.jurisdiction: Meland sokn, Hamre prestegjeld, Hordaland, Norway
planItems.rationale: Primary target: the marriage record of Unna Halsteinsdatter, which names her husband and the marriage date. Search Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 (name-searchable, per the Norway locality entry) on the given-name variants Unna, Una and Unne with the patronymic Halsteinsdatter. The 1763-1810 window runs from about age 18 to the age of 65, since the subject's marriage date is unknown. Hamre kirkebøker hold Meland marriages (Meland_Parish genealogy page). If the marriage is in a later remarriage, the same search will surface it. Each marriage entry names the bride's father and the groom, so a hit that is a second marriage must be checked against the first.

Fallback for item 2. If the indexed marriage search returns nothing, the spelling variants or patronymic may have been recorded differently. Run a full-text co-occurrence search on Unna and Hestdal (both as separate terms, unscoped to a collection) over the Hamre marriage and banns pages. The Norway locality entry notes that recorders set name spellings, so the page text can hold a reading the index does not. This item is the usual route once indexed search has stalled, and it does not assert that any hit is the subject.

planItems.jurisdiction: Meland sokn, Hamre prestegjeld, Hordaland, Norway
planItems.rationale: FAN item: marriages of the subject's siblings, found from the baptisms in item 1. A sibling's marriage entry names the bondsmen, witnesses and the families of the spouses, who are often the same families the subject married into. Search Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 (name-searchable) on each sibling's name. This tests whether the subject's husband appears among the in-laws of her siblings. It depends on the sibling names from item 1, so run it after item 1.

planItems.jurisdiction: Meland sokn, Hamre prestegjeld, Hordaland, Norway
planItems.rationale: Widow's record: if the marriage record is not found, a burial entry for the subject will often name her as the widow of her husband, which gives the husband's name directly. The window runs from after a plausible marriage to a plausible death, given her 1745 birth. The Hamre burial register (Hamre kirkebøker 1677-1928 per the Norway locality entry) is the register covering the subject's home parish. Search on the name variants of item 2 with no surname filter, in case the entry is under the married name.

A household record: if she was married by 1801 (she was then about 55), the 1801 census for Hamre prestegjeld lists her household with the head, who may be her husband. Availability of this census is not confirmed: the collection search for Norway returned no rows this session, so run collections_search for the 1801 Norway census before executing this item. It is a check on the marriage found by items 2 and 3, not a source of the marriage date.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

Elena died after 1718 (she was mother of a child christened that year) and her death date is unknown. Her burial entry in the Barsebäck register may give her age, which bounds her birth year, and may name her home parish or father. Sweden Burials (1649-1920) is name-searchable but partial; the Barsebäck volumes (image groups 004514823, 004514824, covering 1648 onward) are 0% indexed, so browse by year around each death.

Elena's birth parish is unknown, so indexed search on her name alone cannot separate her from other Elenas. A full-text co-occurrence search for Asmund and Elena together, run unscoped, can reach parental or marriage entries that name her father and home parish in the transcribed page text, even where the name index is partial. Treat the patronymic Asmundsdotter as the father being Asmund, not yet a named individual.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. output.text_response:
Mode: supersede. The question is q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?" The active plan pl_002 was superseded and replaced by pl_003, because the reported 1865 death of Thomas Flynn invalidates its 1870-1890 probate window. Nothing in the completed items was changed.

Survey facts the new plan rests on:
- Thomas Flynn (I2) is in the tree with a birth of about 1818 in Ireland, and has three children recorded: Patrick (I1), Mary (I3) and James (I4).
- The 1850 census shows Patrick, age 5, in Thomas's household in Schuylkill County (log_001).
- The 1860 census shows Patrick, age 15, in Thomas's household (log_004). That is consistent with a death around 1865.
- Patrick's 1908 death certificate names Thomas as father (log_005).
- The 1865 death is only the user's reference and has not been verified.
- The old probate item pli_006 was still in progress with no search logged. It is carried forward as pli_007 with the corrected window.

Plan pl_003 for q_001:
1. pli_007, probate, Schuylkill County, 1860-1870, FamilySearch (images). This is an image browse of the Register of Wills dockets, since the collection is browse-only. It looks for a will or administration naming Patrick as a son.
2. pli_008, cemetery, Schuylkill County, 1860-1870, FamilySearch. Name-searchable. It looks for a burial near 1865 that confirms identity.
3. pli_009, church, Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County, 1860-1870, held at the parish or diocese. Fallback for pli_008, because Catholic burials may not appear in the cemetery index.
4. pli_010, census, Schuylkill County, 1870, FamilySearch. Name-searchable. If Thomas is absent and a widow heads a household with Patrick, Mary and James, that supports the 1865 death. If he is present, the reference is wrong.
5. pli_011, military, Pennsylvania, 1861-1865, FamilySearch. A FAN item for James and Patrick, the sons of military age. Enlistment entries may name a father or residence.
6. pli_012, other, Schuylkill County, 1865-1870, FamilySearch. Fallback for pli_007. It looks for a land deed from Thomas's estate that names heirs.
7. pli_013, vital record, Pennsylvania, 1835-1845, FamilySearch. This is the required parentage item for the marriage of Thomas to Patrick's mother. It falls outside the 1860-1870 window because it must predate Patrick's birth of about 1845. The mother's name is not in the tree, so her maiden name depends on whether this was her first marriage.

Two gaps remain. The Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules cover only the census years 1850, 1860, 1870 and 1880, so they would not capture a death in 1865 and were left out. The cemetery and parish items are still unverified for Catholic burials.

The plan now searches Schuylkill County's probate files, cemetery and parish burial records, and the 1870 census for signs of Thomas's death in the 1860s, with the sons' Civil War enlistments and the parents' marriage as supporting checks. The next step is to run the searches, starting with the probate item.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.question: Where did Josiah Rowe (b. ~1828, Ohio) reside between 1850 and 1865, and with whom was he living?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree places Josiah in Vigo County, Indiana at his death in 1879 and gives Ohio as his birthplace, but nothing is documented between his birth and his 1862 enlistment. No records have been searched yet.

planItems.rationale: The 1850 federal census is name-searchable (national collection) and is the first place to fix Josiah's household and co-residents in the window. Josiah is b. about 1828 in Ohio, so he should be age about 22; search on the birth-year range and Ohio birthplace, then read every member of his household. This census names every member but states no relationships, so any relationship must be inferred and labelled as such in later analysis.

The 1860 federal census is name-searchable (national collection) and falls inside the window. Compare his household with the 1850 entry from item 1 to see whether co-residents, the household head and his location changed. 1860 also records birthplace, so it checks the Ohio birth. Like 1850 it names all members without relationships, and neighbours on the same page are FAN leads for item 9.

The tree records Josiah's Indiana military service from 1862 to 1865, and the Civil War and Later Pension Files collection is name-searchable. A pension file for a Union soldier, or for his widow, commonly gives his residence at enlistment, post-war residence and next-of-kin, all of which bear on where he lived in 1862-1865 and with whom. The file runs to 1934, so it is sized to the collection's own range rather than the 1850-1865 window.

The Indiana Military Discharges collection (ca.1864 onward) is name-searchable and may hold Josiah's discharge record, which can state his county of residence at enlistment or at discharge. It runs from the 1864 start, so it can cover only the last part of the window; it is a check on item 3, not a substitute for it.

The Indiana Voter Registers collection (1850-1931) is name-searchable and voter lists are usually kept by precinct, which can place Josiah at a specific township or ward during the window. Use it to test the residence from items 1 and 2 across the full window, not only at the census dates.

The Indiana Marriages collection (1811-2019) is name-searchable. A marriage of Josiah in the window would name his bride and his residence, which answers the with-whom part of the question if he married there. Search his surname in Vigo County and neighbouring counties, because the locality entry shows he may have married before he moved to Terre Haute.

The locality entry says the Vigo County marriage records are not in an indexed collection, so the marriage register must be read from the county clerk, not by collection id. This is the fallback for item 6: if the statewide marriage index shows no entry for Josiah in the window, the county's own register is the next check.

Deeds, mortgages and leases recorded in Vigo County during the window fix Josiah's residence and any household property he shared with a spouse or relatives. The locality entry gives no indexed collection for these, so the county recorder's own books are the source. Read every grantor and grantee name for Josiah and his co-residents from items 1 and 2.

FAN item. The Indiana Church Records collection is name-searchable. Once items 1 and 2 name Josiah's neighbours and co-residents, search these names in church records of the same township. A co-resident who is also a church member can place Josiah in the same congregation and near the same people during the window. Run after items 1 and 2.
